newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Greenpeace pickets U.S. genetic soy ship.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greenpeace pickets U.S. genetic soy ship.

text.p: Greenpeace environmentalists prepared to sail barges to picket a freighter that they think is bringing the first genetically-altered U.S. soybeans to Europe.

Greenpeace campaigners said a high tide and winds in the River Elbe would make it dangerous to try to block the 1900 GMT Hamburg docking of the Ideal Progress, with 44,600 tonnes of new crop soybeans for German processor Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag).
As some one to two percent of the U.S. soybean crop is now made up of genetically-altered beans, Greenpeace says it is likely that some of this material is aboard Ideal Progress.
"We will use this ship's arrival to show Oelag cannot get out of its responsibility for the consumer," spokesman Michael Kuehn said.
Health anxieties about biotechnology are most acute in Germany, where Greenpeace has gathered 120,000 signatories to a consumer petition against modified soybeans.
Developed by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto Co, the soybeans have been altered to resist widely used Roundup weedkiller.
Campaigners want crushers to segregate these beans and for the food industry either to boycott them or at least label products that might be derived from them.
Soya is used in some form or another in some 30,000 foodstuffs including margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
U.S. consumer activist Jeremy Rifkin, who seeks a world boycott of genetically altered grain, arrived in Germany on Tuesday to declare that "this global boycott will not go away."

He said brokers in the U.S. Midwest were already negotiating contracts for a gene-free supply with European processors who did not want Monsanto soy and an initial cargo would sail from Duluth, Minn. in the United States on Tuesday or Wednesday.
The ship reaching Hamburg and others leaving Duluth symbolised rival approaches to the future of farm and food policy, he said.
German Social Democrat MP Liesel Hartenstein said on Tuesday consumers "must not be degraded into guinea pigs." She demanded segregation of soybeans, labelling and more health research.
The government position is that comprehensive labelling should be introduced but that responsible use of biotechnology is good for the farm and food industries.
Some leading firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, already said they will not sell products with oils from modified beans, but they consider the beans safe.
But the Food and Drink Industry Association in the Netherlands, where cargoes will also be landed this month, said in a statement that members would use genetically-altered soya.
"The Dutch food sector only processes and sells products that are safe for the consumer and which have government approval," the Nederlandse Voedingsmiddelen Industrie said.
It said health authorities in the United States, UK, European Union, Canada and Japan had also approved the product.

The United States last year sold two million tonnes of soybeans to Germany worth $690 million. Argentina plans to use modified beans in 1997. Traders said it was possible to buy soy oil guaranteed not to have been made with such beans but cost was a problem.
The Iowa-based firm of Genetic ID, for instance, says it can detect whether foreign DNA has been spliced in to soybeans.
But traders said the tests plus separate transport and storage add about $15 per tonne to the cost of soybeans shipped to Europe. Current prices are around $276 per tonne.
